Editor
Manager

scenario_questions.scenario:
You’re handed a rough channel brief for a B2B SaaS tooling startup with these fragments:

```markdown
Audience (draft): "People who like productivity"
Competitors: "Acme DevTips (10–min devlogs), SprintGuru PM (5–8 min how‑tos)"
Objective: "Book qualified demos; secondary: newsletter signups"
Proposed content: "Daily 45–60s shorts; occasional 40‑min webinars"
Working title: "Ship Faster TV"
Channel promise (tagline): "Tiny tips. Massive change."
Notes: Most topics need explanatory context and screen walkthroughs to be credible.
```
scenario_questions.task: Diagnose the core contradictions in the draft. Propose a corrected audience definition, a niche boundary that differentiates from the listed competitors, revised objectives that are testable, and a channel promise that matches the required content depth and cadence. Justify each change in terms of the homepage experience and first 30 seconds a new visitor sees.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A strong answer identifies that the audience is too broad and should be narrowed (e.g., product managers and tech leads at B2B SaaS with 5–20‑person teams). The niche should be framed against competitors (e.g., "zero‑to‑one PM workflow automation" rather than generic devlogs or mid‑level PM how‑tos). Objectives should be measurable (e.g., X demo bookings/month via trailer CTA and top‑link newsletter signups). The promise should reconcile depth and cadence (e.g., "Twice‑weekly 4–6 minute walkthroughs that automate PM workflows"), supported by a short 45–60s trailer and a top "Start here" playlist. Justification connects these decisions to the homepage layout (short trailer + fundamentals playlist) and explains why shorts‑only would under‑serve credibility for demo bookings.

rubric.criterion: Identifies at least two concrete contradictions (audience vagueness vs objective depth; shorts‑first vs credibility needs)
Proposes a precise, defensible audience and niche boundary relative to competitors
Defines measurable primary/secondary objectives aligned to demo bookings and list growth
Crafts a channel promise matching depth and cadence, and explains how the first‑visit layout supports it
Clarity and coherence of justification (ties to homepage experience within Studio constraints)

scenario_questions.scenario:
A mid‑size company is migrating from a personal YouTube channel to a Brand Account. The org chart:

```text
People
- CMO (wants oversight, not daily ops)
- Brand Designer (assets and QA)
- Content Lead (publishing cadence, playlists)
- Two Video Editors (upload, metadata polish, thumbnails)
- Agency (community management + occasional uploads)
Risks
- Prior channel was owned by a departed employee
- Revenue data is sensitive internally
- Need resilience during holidays
```
scenario_questions.task: Design a permission and governance plan in YouTube Studio that satisfies least‑privilege, protects revenue data, and avoids single‑owner risk. Specify exact roles for each party, 2FA policy, upload defaults, and a light‑weight review workflow that won’t block publication. Explain why your matrix meets each risk.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A good matrix uses a Brand Account with at least two internal Owners (CMO plus Content Lead or IT), Manager role avoided unless necessary; Editors for Video Editors; Editor (limited) for the Agency to hide revenue; Brand Designer as Viewer (or Viewer limited) with asset QA via previews. Enforce 2FA for all roles. Upload defaults set to Private (or Unlisted) with a checklist to flip to Public after review. Review flow: Editors upload and set metadata; Brand Designer reviews thumbnails/banners; Content Lead final approval changes visibility. Rationale addresses revenue privacy (Editor limited), resilience (multiple Owners), and avoiding excessive privileges for the agency.

rubric.criterion: Accurate role assignments per responsibility with least‑privilege rationale
Addresses revenue privacy explicitly (Editor limited usage)
Includes 2FA policy and multiple Owners to avoid single‑point failure
Defines upload defaults and a lightweight review path that supports cadence

practical_tasks.title: Produce the Channel Brief (strategy)
practical_tasks.brief: Create a channel brief that the setup team can execute without re‑asking basics. It must define the audience, niche boundary, measurable objectives, and a clear channel promise. Include the first‑visit experience guidance that translates strategy into how the homepage should look on day one.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A single PDF or Google Doc titled "Channel Brief – <Your Channel Name>".
acceptance_criteria: Audience definition includes at least one primary persona with firmographics/needs relevant to the niche.
Niche boundary names 2–3 competitor channels and states your differentiator in one sentence.
Objectives include 2–3 measurable targets for the first 90 days (e.g., trailer CTR to site, newsletter signups/month).
Channel promise is a single sentence matching required content depth and cadence.
Homepage guidance includes: trailer intent (30–90s), top 2 playlists to feature, and the CTA/link priority (mobile first link order).
Risks/assumptions section lists at least 3 risks (e.g., asset gaps, cadence feasibility) and mitigations.

rubric.criterion: Audience and niche clarity with credible competitor differentiation
Measurable objectives aligned to funnel intent and timeframe
Channel promise that coherently matches depth and cadence
Homepage guidance that is actionable (spotlights, top playlists, link priority)
Risks and mitigations grounded in the brief’s choices

practical_tasks.title: Configure the Channel Plan (branding, layout, permissions, governance)
practical_tasks.brief: Translate the brief into a concrete configuration plan the Studio admin can execute. You are not required to press the buttons in a live channel, but your plan must be specific enough to reproduce in Studio without decisions left open.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A single PDF or Google Doc titled "YouTube Channel Configuration Plan – <Your Channel Name>", plus an assets folder (zipped or drive link) containing avatar(s) and banner(s) at correct sizes.
acceptance_criteria: Permissions matrix lists each role (Owner/Manager/Editor/Editor limited/Viewer) for all participants with rationale and 2FA policy.
Upload defaults specified (visibility, comments moderation level, category) with the intended review workflow and publish flip defined.
Homepage layout documented for unsubscribed and returning viewers: spotlight items and first 4 sections in order, with playlist names.
Branding assets provided: avatar at 800x800 (works at 88x88) and banner at 2560x1440, with text confined to 1546x423 safe area; include a mockup overlay demonstrating safe area usage.
Community governance: comment moderation settings (e.g., hold potentially inappropriate, increase strictness, block links) and blocked words philosophy (examples, not exhaustive lists).
Link plan: banner link order (mobile and desktop considerations) and CTA alignment to objectives.

rubric.criterion: Accurate, least‑privilege permissions matrix with security (2FA, redundancy)
Upload defaults and review workflow that prevent accidental publish yet preserve cadence
Homepage layout that directly reflects the brief’s promise (spotlights + ordered sections)
Branding assets meet size/safe‑area constraints and show legibility across devices
Community settings and link plan align with objectives and mobile constraints

Thu 9, Reviews, Long, Budget Drill Review, Mira, Script

scenario_questions.task: Propose specific moderation settings and checklist updates that reduce visible spam within the first hour while minimizing false positives and preserving engagement. Include changes to blocked words, hold settings, and any pre-publish steps.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Proposed controls: Pre-publish, enable Comments: Hold potentially inappropriate comments for review and toggle Increase strictness. Expand Blocked words with targeted variants ("fr€e", "g1veaway", common spacing like "f r e e"), plus a link-shortener list (bit.ly, t.co, tinyurl, ow.ly). concept_mcqs.stem:
You open Retention for a 7:40 video and see:
```text
Audience retention (first 60s) for Video A
00:00 100%
00:10 78%
00:20 62%
00:30 55%
00:45 53%
01:00 52%
"Key moments": viewers sped up at 00:03–00:07
Opening:
00:00–00:08 animated logo sting
00:08–00:13 "In this video we will..."
00:13 first on-screen demo step
```
You can only change the first 15 seconds. Which change is most likely to lift average view duration by reducing early drop-off?
options: Remove the 8s logo and cold open with the demo’s payoff in the first 3s, then state the promise while showing progress.
Enable the first mid-roll ad at 00:30 to monetize earlier and keep viewers engaged.
Add a card at 00:12 linking to the full playlist so viewers have an exit to more of your content.
Add subtitles and a pinned comment with timestamps to help skimmers navigate.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The sharp early drop aligns with a long logo + generic promise before any payoff. Starting with the result/hook in the first seconds addresses hook loss directly and is the highest-leverage retention fix.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Cards at 00:12 create an exit during the fragile first 15s, likely worsening retention. C: Earlier mid-rolls cannot be placed before 8 minutes for most videos and, even if possible, ads do not fix an early content hook problem. D: Subtitles and timestamps help accessibility and navigation but do not remove the dead time that causes the drop.

concept_mcqs.stem:
From Advanced Analytics (last 28 days):
```csv
Traffic Source,Impressions,CTR,Avg view duration,Views
Browse features,1,200,000,2.0%,5:10,24,000
Suggested videos,800,000,4.9%,4:02,39,200
YouTube search,400,000,6.1%,3:15,24,400
```
You want to grow reach from Browse without harming engagement. What is the best next action?
options: Add more tags to include trending keywords so YouTube better understands your topic.
Shorten all videos to under 3 minutes to raise average view duration percentage.
Revise thumbnails to emphasize the payoff with less text, then run a Studio Test & Compare to validate CTR lift on Browse.
Move upload time two hours earlier so the video hits Browse sooner and accumulates momentum.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Browse CTR is weak relative to other sources. Thumbnails dominate Browse decisioning. Systematically testing stronger payoff-led thumbnails directly targets CTR on Browse while guarding against engagement harm by measuring watch time per impression.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Tags have minimal impact on Browse visibility; metadata tweaks won’t fix a thumbnail-driven CTR issue. C: Shortening indiscriminately can reduce absolute watch time and may not fix Browse CTR. D: Timing may matter at the margin, but the core issue is low CTR on home feed creative, not publish hour.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You ran a YouTube Studio Test & Compare on two thumbnails for the same video. After 6 hours:
```text
Variant A: 8,200 impressions, CTR 4.6%, views 377, avg view dur 3:42
Variant B: 6,900 impressions, CTR 6.7% (+2.1pp vs A), views 462, avg view dur 3:35
Audience geography during test window:
A: 62% US, 18% UK, 10% CA
B: 38% US, 27% IN, 15% PH
Test window: Tue 09:00–15:00 local
```
What’s the correct call?
options: Repeat the test but change titles and thumbnails together to maximize the effect size.
Stop the test; the lower average view duration on B means it harms watch time despite CTR.
Extend the test to at least 48–72 hours to average out daypart and geography effects before calling it.
Declare B the winner and roll it out immediately because of a +2.1pp CTR advantage.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The sample is short and audience mix differs between variants, which can bias CTR. Extending across dayparts and geos improves reliability. Watch time per impression should be checked over a longer window too.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: The CTR gap may be sampling noise or geo-driven; calling early risks a false win. C: The small AVD difference over 6 hours is inconclusive; judge on watch time per impression after a stable run. D: Changing two variables breaks attribution; you wouldn’t know which element drove results.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Audience tab shows:
```text
When your viewers are on YouTube (local time)
Peak blocks: Tue–Thu 18:00–21:00 (darkest), Fri 17:00–19:00 (dark)
HD processing for your 4K uploads: ~20–30 minutes
Notifications: most effective within 5 minutes of publish
```
You plan a premiere on Thursday. What timing approach best uses this insight?
options: Publish at 16:30 Thu to build momentum before peak and let the algorithm pick it up by 18:00.
Publish at 21:00 Thu to maximize competition so the algorithm judges your video against the strongest titles.
Upload at 17:59 Thu and publish immediately at 18:00 so notifications hit exactly at peak start.
Upload hours earlier and schedule the premiere to start at 18:05 Thu; post a Community teaser 45 minutes before.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Uploading early and scheduling slightly into peak ensures processing is complete and notifications land when most viewers are active. A teaser primes awareness before the window.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Processing may still be underway, risking poor initial quality and lower CTR/retention. C: Publishing well before peak leaks notifications and early session starts into a weaker period. D: Publishing at the tail of peak reduces available active viewers and is not a sensible strategy.

concept_mcqs.stem:
At 19:05 you post a Community poll that links to Video X. Realtime shows a spike at 19:06 with these sources increasing:
```text
Traffic sources (last 60 minutes)
Channel pages: +420 views
Notifications: +160 views
External: +8 views
Browse features: flat
```
How should you attribute the spike?
options: Mostly Community post clicks counted under Channel pages, plus some subscriber notifications; not External.
Mostly Browse features because home feed shows polls to non-subscribers.
Primarily External because Community posts are web links outside YouTube.
Evenly split across Suggested and Search because viewers type in the title after seeing the post.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Community post engagement typically reflects as Channel pages traffic; subscribers pinged by the post may also appear under Notifications. External would be minimal unless linking off-platform.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Community posts are an on-platform surface, not External. C: While polls can surface broadly, the immediate spike aligns with Channel pages/Notifications, not Browse. D: Some may search later, but the real-time spike is not evenly split that way.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Last 14 days Monetization tab:
```text
Date range split: Before vs After marking 6 videos as "Made for kids"
RPM: $2.90  ->  $0.98
Views: 210,000 -> 205,000
Watch time (hrs): 7,100 -> 6,900
Top ad suitability setting: "Made for kids" on affected videos
Comments: disabled on affected videos
```
What’s the primary driver of the RPM drop?
options: RPM fell because comments were disabled, which directly reduces ad rates.
Personalized ads are limited on Made for Kids content, lowering RPM even with similar views.
Audience shifted to lower-CPM geographies; the mark is unrelated.
Shorter average view duration reduced mid-roll fill rate on sub-8-minute videos.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Marking content as Made for Kids restricts personalized ads and certain formats, which typically lowers RPM independent of view volume.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Geo shifts can matter, but the coincident policy change is the stronger, stated cause. C: Comments do not directly affect RPM. D: Mid-rolls are not applicable to sub‑8‑minute videos and the data does not show a duration change driving the drop.

concept_mcqs.stem:
End screen element report (last 90 days):
```csv
Video,End screen CTR,Elements shown,Element clicks leading to next video,Avg view duration (next video)
A,0.3%,4,42,4:10
B,1.1%,2,210,5:05
C,0.6%,4,88,3:30
```
You want to maximize session watch time from Video A. What’s the best change?
options: Reduce end screen to 1–2 tightly relevant video elements and start it in the last 15 seconds.
Add links to your channel homepage and subscribe to increase overall exits.
Extend the end screen to 30 seconds so viewers have more time to choose.
Insert a card earlier at 50% watch to send viewers to any high-performing video.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Fewer, highly relevant options started in the final moments typically lift end screen CTR and continuation to the next video, improving session watch time.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Channel and subscribe elements don’t directly continue a viewing session. C: Early cards can siphon viewers mid‑watch, hurting AVD. D: Overlong end screens create dead time and can increase drop‑offs.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Audience tab summary (last 90 days):
```text
New viewers: 72%
Returning viewers: 28%
Avg time between episodes in your main series: 3 weeks
Playlist starts -> Episode 2 retention at 30%: 41%
Upload cadence: 2 uploads/month
```
For the next 90 days, which action most directly improves returning viewers for the series?
options: Run a monthly giveaway in comments to incentivize returns.
Increase to a weekly episode cadence, front-stack the playlist order by narrative, and tease next episode in the end screen.
Translate descriptions into 5 languages to widen reach.
Switch entirely to Shorts to boost frequency without changing the series plan.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Returnership in series content responds to predictable cadence, strong sequencing, and explicit next‑episode cues that create habits.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Giveaways can spike one-off comments but rarely build viewing habits. C: Shorts can grow top‑of‑funnel but won’t by themselves improve series completion/return for long‑form. D: Translation helps reach but not habit formation for your current audience.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You plan a subscriber milestone celebration. Draft giveaway mechanic A requires commenters to post the same hashtag daily for a week to qualify. Mechanic B uses a Community post linking to a simple form, one entry per person, with clear rules and disclosure.
Which approach better aligns with policy and community health while still driving engagement?
options: Neither; giveaways are prohibited on YouTube and will result in strikes.
Mechanic B: a Community post plus external form, one entry per person, clear rules and disclosure.
Mechanic A: repeated comment hashtagging to maximize engagement signals on each video.
Mechanic A but with comments held for review so spam won’t be public.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Mechanic B avoids incentivizing repetitive/spammy comments, provides clear rules, and uses the Community tab appropriately while protecting discussion quality.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Incentivizing repetitive comments risks spam and policy issues, harming community health. C: Holding for review doesn’t fix the underlying incentive to spam. D: Giveaways are allowed if they follow policies; claiming they’re prohibited is incorrect.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Two candidates to feature in end screens for subscriber growth:
```csv
Video,Unique viewers,Subscribers gained from this video
How to X (A),50,000,500
How to Y (B),20,000,420
```
Which do you feature to maximize subscriber conversions from end screen traffic, and why?
options: Don’t feature either; end screens should only promote playlists, not single videos, for subs.
Feature both equally; conversion rate is irrelevant for end screens.
Feature Video A; it has more uniques and therefore more headroom for subs even at a lower rate.
Feature Video B; its subscriber conversion rate is ~2.1% vs A’s ~1.0%, so it’s more efficient at turning viewers into subs.
concept_mcqs.explanation: End screens reach a small, intentful cohort. Promoting the asset with the higher sub‑per‑viewer rate yields more subs per end screen click.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Volume alone doesn’t beat efficiency when end screen exposure is scarce. C: Conversion rate is central to this choice. D: Playlists can be useful, but single high‑converting videos are valid and often better for subs.

scenario_questions.scenario:
Your last 28‑day Analytics split shows the following:
```text
Long‑form (6–12 min)
Impressions 1.8M | CTR 4.1% | Views 73k | Avg view dur 5:02 | Watch time 6,130h
New:returning 58:42 | Subs gained 1,050 | Top source: Suggested (5.1% CTR)

Shorts (15–45s)
Views 1.2M | Avg view dur 17s | % swiped away in first 3s: 52%
Subs gained 2,400 | Top source: Shorts feed

Channel‑level
Returning viewers +8% MoM | Unique viewers 420k | End screen CTR 0.7%
```
You have 90 days to grow reach and set up for monetisation readiness. Budget allows 3 uploads/week total. You can mix formats. You cannot hire editors.
scenario_questions.task: Decide your allocation between Shorts and long‑form for the next 90 days, and specify how you will connect Shorts to long‑form to compound watch time and subs. Justify with the data above, and state 3 success metrics with target ranges for day 30, 60, and 90.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A strong answer allocates a mix that exploits Shorts for top‑of‑funnel while protecting long‑form watch time and habit formation. For example: 2 Shorts + 1 long‑form per week for 6 weeks, then evaluate; pivot to 1 Short + 2 long‑form if returning viewers lag. Rationale: Long‑form delivers 6,130h with only 73k views, so watch time per view is high; Shorts add 2,400 subs but weak session depth and high 3s swipe‑aways. Connectors: produce Shorts cut‑downs with a direct promise of value in the first 1–2s and a visual CTA to the related long‑form; add long‑form end screens referencing the series; use Community posts to bridge days between uploads. Define metrics: watch time hours (target +20% by day 60, +35% by day 90), returning viewers share (target 42% -> 48% by day 60), Shorts 3s swipe‑away rate down from 52% to <40%, end screen CTR from 0.7% to >1.2%, subs gained per long‑form view up 20%. Note constraints and risks (editing capacity), and plan a 4‑week review cadence with pre‑registered thresholds to reallocate slots.

rubric.criterion: Clear allocation across formats with cadence and time phasing tied to capacity
Justification grounded in provided metrics (watch time per view, CTR, swipe‑away, returning viewers)
Concrete cross‑format connection tactics (Shorts to long‑form), not just generic promotion
Three measurable success metrics with realistic target ranges and time checkpoints

scenario_questions.scenario: You are launching a 6‑episode tutorial series, one per week. The last series suffered from misleading thumbnails and uneven performance across geographies. A holiday in week 3 skews US traffic. You have access to YouTube’s Test & Compare for thumbnails and titles.
scenario_questions.task: Design an A/B testing plan for thumbnails and titles that avoids confounding. Specify hypothesis, primary metric, guardrail metric, randomization, minimum test duration/sample, and decision thresholds. Include how you’ll handle the holiday effect.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Example plan: Hypothesis: a close‑up with the solved outcome and minimal text (“Done in 3 steps”) increases Browse CTR without reducing watch time per impression. Primary metric: CTR on Browse features. Guardrail: watch time per impression and average view duration do not decline >3%. Randomization: use Studio Test & Compare with 50/50 traffic split per video, testing thumbnails only for episodes 1–2; freeze titles. Minimum duration: at least 72 hours and 20k impressions per variant spanning two peak cycles; rerun in episode 4 for titles while fixing the winning thumbnail design from episodes 1–2. Decision threshold: call a winner if CTR uplift ≥1.5pp with guardrail within bounds and results stable across geographies (±0.5pp). Handle holiday: exclude US holiday window from decision or extend test to capture a comparable post‑holiday weekday; segment by geography before calling.

rubric.criterion: Specific hypothesis mapped to a single variable per test phase (thumbnail then title)
Primary and guardrail metrics appropriate to the objective (CTR vs watch time per impression)
Sound randomization, minimum duration/sample size, and decision thresholds
Explicit handling of the holiday/geography confound

scenario_questions.scenario:
Comment moderation over the last month:
```text
Avg creator reply time: 3 days
% comments with questions unanswered after 48h: 61%
Toxicity flags: 4% (auto‑held), 1 strike warning for repeated spam replies by fans in a giveaway
Top comment themes: requests for deeper dives; confusion in step 3; praise for pacing
```
Your goal is to improve engagement quality and reduce friction for prospective returners.
scenario_questions.task: Propose a 90‑day community operations plan covering: response SLAs, moderation workflow (roles and tools), weekly Community posts and polls cadence with topics, and how you will measure success. Include one tactic to turn high‑quality Q&A into content.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Plan with a 24h response SLA for questions, 72h for general comments; assign a moderator (Viewer role) plus one Editor to pin/heart, with daily 30‑minute blocks post‑publish and a weekend sweep. Enable filters for links and common spam phrases; document escalation for toxicity. Cadence: 1 Community post/week (behind‑the‑scenes, progress updates), 1 poll/week (next topic choice, pain points). Pin a clarifying comment under tutorials addressing step 3 confusion; compile repeated Q&As into a monthly FAQ video or chaptered update. Success metrics: median reply time <24h, % answered within 48h to >85%, increase likes/comment by 20%, reduce auto‑held to <2% through guidance, lift returning viewers by +5pp over baseline.

rubric.criterion: Operational response SLAs and staffing/roles (incl. User Management use)
Clear moderation workflow with prevention and escalation steps
Community post/poll cadence with substantive, on‑topic ideas
Measurement plan with at least two engagement and one retention metric

scenario_questions.scenario:
Monetisation readiness audit for three videos:
```text
V1: 9:20 tutorial. First 5s include repeated strong profanity used for emphasis. Self‑certified "strong profanity in opening minute". Limited ads.
V2: 8:05 compilation of TikTok clips with minimal voiceover reactions; no licenses; reused watermark visible.
V3: 12:40 review with affiliate links in description; verbal disclosure at 00:30 and #ad in description.
```
Channel goal: maximise eligibility and avoid future limited ads/reuse rejections.
scenario_questions.task: Identify the two largest risks and propose concrete remediation steps to make the videos eligible without materially harming performance. Explain any trade‑offs.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Largest risks: V1 ad suitability (strong profanity in opening seconds) and V2 reuse without transformation/licenses. Remedies: For V1, re‑edit to remove or bleep profanity in the opening; shift any strong language away from the opening minute and reduce frequency overall; re‑self‑certify and request review. Trade‑off: slightly altered tone but better green icon consistency. For V2, either obtain licenses for all clips and add substantial transformative commentary (on‑screen analysis, pause and explain, chapters), or replace reused segments with original examples; remove watermarks. Trade‑off: more production time and potentially lower raw click appeal, but resolves reuse risk. V3 is generally fine with clear disclosures; ensure links comply with policies and add context in description; monitor for spammy formatting.

rubric.criterion: Correct identification of primary risks (opening profanity; reused content without transformation/licensing)
Concrete, policy‑aligned remediation steps for each risky video
Acknowledgement of performance trade‑offs and how to mitigate them
